nameStory: Micrasterias gets its name from the Greek words 'micro' meaning small and 'asterias' meaning star, referring to its beautiful star-like shape when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'floridensis' suggests it was first described from Florida, though these tiny aquatic gems can be found in freshwater habitats much farther north.
description: Micrasterias floridensis is a microscopic single-celled organism called a desmid that lives in freshwater. While you can't see individual cells with the naked eye, they sometimes form visible green films or masses in clean ponds and lakes. Each cell is symmetrical and star-shaped, split into two identical halves connected at the center. These tiny beauties are only about 0.1 millimeters across - smaller than the period at the end of this sentence.

idTips.label: Microscopic nature
idTips.description: Individual organisms are invisible to the naked eye and require at least 100x magnification to see clearly - they appear as intricate, symmetrical star-like shapes

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Appears bright green under the microscope due to chlorophyll, and may form pale green films or scums on water surfaces when abundant

idTips.label: Symmetrical shape
idTips.description: Each cell is perfectly symmetrical with two identical halves joined at a narrow center, creating an elaborate star or snowflake pattern

idTips.label: Clean water indicator
idTips.description: Found only in clean, unpolluted freshwater - their presence indicates good water quality

habitat: Lives in clean, still or slow-moving freshwater including ponds, lakes, marshes, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England. Prefers slightly acidic to neutral water with low nutrient levels. Often found among other aquatic plants or floating near the surface in areas with good light penetration.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms and daylight increases. May start forming visible green films on pond surfaces in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when most likely to be noticed as green scums or films on clean pond surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Populations decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases. May still be present but less abundant and harder to spot.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very low numbers under ice cover. Some cells may survive as resistant spores in sediments.

funFact: Despite being single-celled organisms smaller than a grain of sand, Micrasterias cells are living works of art - each one grows its elaborate star pattern from the center outward, with the two halves developing in perfect mirror-image symmetry like a biological snowflake.
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other desmid species that also form green films on water, but Micrasterias species have distinctly star-shaped, deeply divided cells rather than the crescent shapes of Closterium or the simple ovals of Cosmarium. Remember: Micrasterias makes magnificent stars under the microscope.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'algae' by many, desmids like Micrasterias are more closely related to land plants than to other groups commonly called algae. They're considered among the most beautiful of all microscopic life forms and are prized by microscopists for their intricate, jewel-like appearance.
compareHints: Micrasterias floridensis differs from other Micrasterias species mainly in the specific details of its star-shaped lobes and projections - features that require expert microscopic examination to distinguish. Compared to its relatives like M. truncata or M. rotata, M. floridensis has its own unique pattern of cell wall ornamentation and lobe shapes. All Micrasterias species share the same basic symmetrical, star-like form that sets them apart from other desmids.
